quiz.question: Why is a modular monolith recommended over 10 separate microservices for the initial Learning Platform Capstone?
options: Spring Boot cannot connect to PostgreSQL from microservices
It provides clearly separated business modules inside one deployable service, demonstrating transactions, security, caching, and async messaging without premature distributed-system complexity
Microservices do not support JWT authentication
Docker only runs a single container
quiz.explanation: A modular monolith keeps strong module boundaries while avoiding unnecessary network hops, distributed transactions, and operational overhead early on.

quiz.question: Why must the backend ignore any role field sent by the client during public student registration?
options: Because PostgreSQL cannot store ENUM values
To prevent privilege escalation where an attacker registers themselves as an ADMIN; the server must always assign the default STUDENT role
Because Spring Security disables POST requests with roles
To reduce JSON payload size
quiz.explanation: Public registration endpoints must hardcode or enforce the default STUDENT role server-side so clients cannot self-provision administrative access.

quiz.question: Why is a PostgreSQL UNIQUE (student_id, course_id) constraint still required on the enrollments table even when the service checks existsByStudentIdAndCourseId(...) first?
options: Spring Data JPA ignores existsBy queries
Two concurrent HTTP requests can both pass the initial existence check before either commits; the database constraint guarantees no duplicate enrollment is persisted
Unique constraints speed up password hashing
PostgreSQL requires unique constraints on every foreign key
quiz.explanation: Application-level existence checks are vulnerable to race conditions under concurrency; a database unique constraint enforces data integrity atomically.

quiz.question: How does the Transactional Outbox Pattern solve the dual-write problem between PostgreSQL and RabbitMQ during enrollment?
options: It stores enrollments inside RabbitMQ instead of PostgreSQL
It saves the enrollment and the outbox_events row in the same PostgreSQL transaction, and a background publisher reliably forwards committed events to RabbitMQ
It disables database transactions when RabbitMQ is enabled
It retries HTTP requests from the browser
quiz.explanation: Because both writes share one ACID transaction, either both commit or both roll back, eliminating lost events or phantom notifications.

quiz.question: Why should the notification consumer in RabbitMQ track processed event IDs and operate idempotently?
options: RabbitMQ guarantees at-least-once delivery, meaning a message can be delivered more than once (e.g., if an acknowledgement is lost)
RabbitMQ deletes messages before consumers read them
PostgreSQL cannot generate UUIDs
Idempotency disables dead-letter queues
quiz.explanation: At-least-once messaging requires duplicate-safe consumers so redelivered events do not send duplicate notifications.

quiz.question: Which data in the Learning Platform API is a good candidate for Redis cache-aside caching, and what must happen when an admin updates a course?
options: Cache raw passwords and JWT secrets in Redis; never evict them
Cache published course details and public listings in Redis, and explicitly evict affected course and listing cache entries on admin updates
Cache every user's private progress indefinitely without TTL
Use Redis as the sole database without PostgreSQL
quiz.explanation: Read-heavy public course metadata benefits from Redis caching, while explicit eviction and TTLs prevent stale data after admin edits.

quiz.question: Why should rate limiting for login and public endpoints be backed by Redis instead of an in-memory map inside each Spring Boot instance?
options: Java HashMaps cannot store integers
When multiple backend instances run behind a load balancer, Redis provides shared, consistent rate-limit counters across all instances
In-memory maps bypass HTTPS
Redis automatically hashes BCrypt passwords
quiz.explanation: Distributed deployments need shared state in Redis so attackers cannot multiply their allowed request quota across instances.

quiz.question: How should the Learning Platform API prevent BOLA (Broken Object Level Authorization) on student progress and enrollment endpoints?
options: Use sequential integer IDs in URLs
Derive the current user ID from the authenticated principal and verify resource ownership (or ADMIN authorization) before returning or modifying records
Hide endpoints from Swagger UI
Validate ownership only in the React frontend
quiz.explanation: Deriving identity from the verified token/principal and enforcing server-side ownership checks stops users from accessing another student's records.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of using Spring ProblemDetail with @RestControllerAdvice across the capstone API?
options: To return raw Java stack traces and SQL queries to clients
To provide a consistent, standardized HTTP error response format across all endpoints without duplicating try/catch logic or leaking internals
To replace PostgreSQL foreign keys
To disable Jakarta Bean Validation
quiz.explanation: Centralized exception handling with ProblemDetail gives clients predictable error payloads (status, code, fieldErrors, traceId) while protecting internal details.

quiz.question: In the recommended 10-phase capstone roadmap, why should automated tests and OpenAPI documentation be written alongside each feature phase rather than left until the end?
options: Because Maven refuses to compile without Swagger UI
Building tests and API contracts per feature verifies correctness, security, and schema integrity incrementally before dependent modules are layered on top
Because Flyway only runs once per project
Because Docker cannot run unit tests
quiz.explanation: Incremental verification ensures authentication, permissions, and database constraints work reliably before subsequent modules build on them.
